questions.q: What does the least-squares line of best fit minimize?
options: The sum of the residuals (vertical errors)
The sum of the **squared** vertical residuals (equivalently, the MSE)
The total plain length of the red error lines
The number of points not on the line
questions.explain: Least squares minimizes $\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$. Plain residuals can cancel ($+5$ and $-5$ sum to $0$); minimizing absolute lengths gives a different "least absolute deviations" line.

questions.q: Fit a least-squares line $y = mx + b$ to the points $(1, 2)$, $(2, 3)$, $(3, 5)$.
questions.explain: $\bar{x} = 2$, $\bar{y} = 10/3$. $m = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5$ and $b = \bar{y} - m\bar{x} = 10/3 - 3 = 1/3$. The line always passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.

questions.q: Under MSE, one point has error $1$ and another has error $5$. How do their penalties compare?
options: They are the same after averaging
questions.explain: Squaring turns $5$ into $25$. That is why a single far-away outlier can swing the whole line: the model bends to avoid one huge squared penalty.

questions.q: In the ML analogy for $y = mx + b$, what are the slope $m$ and intercept $b$?
options: $m$ is the weight, $b$ is the bias
$m$ is the bias, $b$ is the weight
$m$ is the loss, $b$ is the learning rate
questions.explain: The line is the model: slope = weight, intercept = bias. Training adjusts them to minimize the loss — a network does the same with many weights via gradient descent instead of a closed-form formula.
